reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India national programmes
clinicalPearls: Results from ingestion of Taenia solium eggs, which develop into larval cysts (cysticerci) in human tissues; this is distinct from intestinal tapeworm infection acquired by eating undercooked pork
Faecal-oral spread of eggs from a tapeworm carrier means infection can occur even in people who do not eat pork, including through contaminated food and poor sanitation
Cysts lodge preferentially in muscle, subcutaneous tissue, the eyes and the central nervous system; neurological involvement is the most important form
Subcutaneous and muscular cysts may be palpable as painless nodules and can calcify, sometimes visible on imaging
Ocular cysticercosis can threaten vision and requires careful assessment before any antiparasitic therapy
It is a major public-health problem in India and other regions where pigs are raised with poor sanitation
Serology (antibody detection) supports the diagnosis, but imaging is central to defining cyst location and burden
Antiparasitic therapy is used with adjunctive corticosteroids to control the inflammation provoked by dying cysts, and treatment decisions depend heavily on the site and stage of cysts
reference.pathophysiology: When humans ingest Taenia solium eggs, oncospheres hatch in the intestine, penetrate the mucosa and disseminate through the bloodstream to tissues, where they mature into fluid-filled cysticerci. Living cysts often provoke little inflammation, but as they degenerate they release antigens that trigger a host inflammatory and immune response. This inflammation, together with mass effect and eventual calcification, produces most of the clinical manifestations, especially when cysts lie within the brain or eye.
additionalDifferentials: Other soft-tissue parasitic cysts (e.g. hydatid disease)
Lipomas or other benign subcutaneous nodules
Tuberculoma when brain lesions are present
infectionMimics: Tuberculosis with tissue or CNS involvement
additionalInvestigations: CT or MRI to localise and stage cysts, particularly in the brain
Serological antibody or antigen assays (e.g. EITB) as supportive evidence
Ophthalmological examination to exclude ocular cysts before therapy
Plain radiography or ultrasound to detect calcified muscular/subcutaneous cysts
Stool examination for Taenia eggs to identify a coexisting tapeworm carrier
redFlags: New-onset seizures or focal neurological deficits indicating central nervous system involvement
Features of raised intracranial pressure requiring urgent evaluation
Visual disturbance suggesting an ocular cyst that could be harmed by antiparasitic-induced inflammation
Rapid neurological deterioration during or after starting antiparasitic therapy
reference.prognosis: Isolated subcutaneous or muscular cysticercosis is generally benign and often asymptomatic. Prognosis is largely determined by neurological and ocular involvement, where outcome depends on cyst location, number, and the inflammatory response to treatment; many patients do well but some suffer chronic epilepsy or visual loss.
pitfalls: Starting antiparasitic drugs without first excluding ocular cysts, risking sight-threatening inflammation
Overlooking a coexisting intestinal tapeworm that perpetuates transmission
Attributing all soft-tissue nodules to benign causes without imaging in endemic areas
Failing to give adjunctive anti-inflammatory cover when treating heavy or CNS cyst burdens
management: Treat viable parenchymal neurocysticercosis with antiparasitic albendazole, adding praziquantel for heavy cyst burden, always under corticosteroid cover to blunt the inflammatory response to dying cysts
Give corticosteroids during and around antiparasitic therapy to control cyst-degeneration inflammation and cerebral oedema
Control seizures with antiepileptic drugs, the mainstay of symptomatic neurocysticercosis care
Arrange ophthalmological assessment before any antiparasitic therapy and manage ocular cysts surgically, since drug-induced inflammation can destroy vision
Undertake neurosurgical intervention for hydrocephalus with cerebrospinal fluid diversion or shunting, and for intraventricular or large space-occupying cysts
Identify and treat any coexisting intestinal Taenia solium carrier with niclosamide or praziquantel, and screen close household contacts to interrupt faecal-oral transmission
Coordinate infectious diseases, neurology, neurosurgery and ophthalmology, and support sanitation and public-health measures

valueTables.title: Diagnostic criteria for human cysticercosis

cells.text: Cysticerci shown on histologic or microscopic examination of biopsy material; parasite seen in the eye on funduscopy; neuroradiologic demonstration of cystic lesions containing a characteristic scolex

Neuroradiologic lesions suggestive of neurocysticercosis; antibodies to cysticerci in serum by enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot; spontaneous resolution of intracranial cystic lesions, or resolution after albendazole or praziquantel alone

Lesions compatible with neurocysticercosis on neuroimaging; clinical manifestations suggestive of neurocysticercosis; antibodies to cysticerci or cysticercal antigen in cerebrospinal fluid by ELISA; cysticercosis outside the CNS (for example cigar-shaped soft-tissue calcifications)
Residence in a cysticercosis-endemic area; frequent travel to an endemic area; household contact with a person infected with Taenia solium
